newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF revises Bulgaria banks' capital adequacy rules.
newsitem.headline: IMF revises Bulgaria banks' capital adequacy rules.

text.p: Bulgarian commercial banks will be expected to reach a capital to risk assets ratio of six percent by year end instead of the 12 percent previously suggested by the IMF, a central bank official said on Tuesday.

"Arrangements for banks' capital adequacy agreed with the IMF are more realistic now and were modified because of lack of clearly identified sources of financing so far," the official who declined to be named told Reuters.
According to Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) figures, around half of Bulgaria's operating banks estimate their capital to risk assets ratio close to six percent.

On Monday IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk said that measures would be taken to overhaul the Bulgarian banking system before a currency board was introduced in June and about $50 million would be available in the period immediately ahead.
Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski said on Tuesday this money would be provided by state-owned Bulbank.

A report prepared by an IMF mission in December last year put financial support needed to boost banks' capital base to international standards and to assure bank liquidity and operations under a currency board at $151 million.

"So far we are relying on external financing and before introduction of a currency board Bulgaria could reach an agreement with the World Bank to finance part of the programme," a Bank Consolidation Company (BCC) official said.
The BCC was set up in 1992 to manage state equity in local commercial banks. Last year in line with Bulgaria's commitments to international lenders the BCC set bank privatisation as a main priority.
"So far international lenders were more willing to finance banks' recapitalisation only if it was considered as a step towards bank privatisation," the BCC official said.

Under arrangements with the IMF, Bulgarian banks have to cover capital-to-risk assets ratio requirements as follows: eight percent by end of June 1998, 10 percent by end of 1998, 12 percent by the end of June 1999.
Under current BNB regulations local banks had been expected to reach the international standard of eight percent capital to assets ratio by 2001.

According to the memorandum, Bulgaria must impose measures to stabilise weaker state-owned banks in a way deemed satisfactory by the IMF, before the Fund executive board meets in the second week of April to approve the programme.
From past talks with the IMF mission it was clear that international experts consider weak two of six state-owned banks operating now, a BCC official said.
Under BCC estimations only one of the two showed negative net worth of capital. The other one could be stabilised through selling part of its dollar-denominated assets, the official added.

Under the IMF recommendation for two weaker state banks, Bulgaria might seek management contracts with reputable foreign institutions with a mandate to downsize and prepare them for privatisation. -- Sofia Newsroom +359-2 981 8569
